Quality control and preprocessing

Source: vignettes/filtering_subsetting.Rmd
filtering_subsetting.Rmd

Preprocessing steps describe changes to the data stored in a recipe. Adding a step does not execute it: prep() applies preprocessing in the configured order, before running differential-abundance methods. A recipe without a statistical model is valid for preprocessing alone.

The examples below use the included data and run only preprocessing, not statistical models. The thresholds illustrate the API; they are not universal recommendations for microbiome studies.

Inspect overall and grouped QC 

library(dar)
data("metaHIV_phy", package = "dar")

rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy)
recipe_qc(rec)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 13
#>   group_by group     n n_zero pct_zero pct_all_zero pct_singletons
#>   <chr>    <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 NA       NA    70356  57632     81.9            0           20.6
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: pct_doubletons <dbl>, n_samples <dbl>,
#> #   lib_size_min <dbl>, lib_size_max <dbl>, count_mean <dbl>, count_max <dbl>
recipe_qc(rec, group_by = "RiskGroup2")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 13
#>   group_by   group     n n_zero pct_zero pct_all_zero pct_singletons
#>   <chr>      <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 NA         NA    70356  57632     81.9          0             20.6
#> 2 RiskGroup2 hts   18491  15108     81.7         24.2           22.8
#> 3 RiskGroup2 msm   45100  37019     82.1         16.0           20.2
#> 4 RiskGroup2 pwid   6765   5505     81.4         41.2           16.6
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: pct_doubletons <dbl>, n_samples <dbl>,
#> #   lib_size_min <dbl>, lib_size_max <dbl>, count_mean <dbl>, count_max <dbl>

recipe_qc() summarizes the stored abundance matrix independently of any model. It reports sample counts, sparsity, taxa detected in zero, one or two samples, and library-size and count summaries. Singleton and doubleton metrics refer to the number of samples with a detection, not to a taxon’s total read count. The n column counts matrix entries, not biological replicates.

With group_by, the overall row is followed by one row per observed metadata group. The overall row has missing group_by and group identifiers; it is not a group called "all". Grouping is explicit and is not inferred from the statistical target.

Use these summaries to inspect depth or sparsity differences between groups. They do not establish the absence of confounding or that a particular filter will improve statistical accuracy.

Define and apply a shared preprocessing sequence

Here we first retain Bacteria and Archaea, then keep taxa observed in more than 3% of samples. These operations act on the stored features; selecting a rank later with add_model() determines the taxonomic analysis view used by the DA methods.

filtered_rec <- rec |>
  step_subset_taxa(
    tax_level = "Kingdom", taxa = c("Bacteria", "Archaea")
  ) |>
  step_filter_by_prevalence(threshold = 0.03)

filtered <- prep(filtered_rec, parallel = FALSE)

step_subset_taxa() matches annotations at the specified rank. The prevalence filter then uses all samples in the recipe, not one threshold calculated separately within each QC group. Preprocessing preserves the original input object; the prepared recipe contains the filtered data.

Compare the stored data before and after preprocessing:

data.frame(
  stage = c("before", "after"),
  n_taxa = c(nrow(dar::otu_table(rec)), nrow(dar::otu_table(filtered)))
)
#>    stage n_taxa
#> 1 before    451
#> 2  after    278
recipe_qc(filtered)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 13
#>   group_by group     n n_zero pct_zero pct_all_zero pct_singletons
#>   <chr>    <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 NA       NA    43368  30986     71.4            0              0
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: pct_doubletons <dbl>, n_samples <dbl>,
#> #   lib_size_min <dbl>, lib_size_max <dbl>, count_mean <dbl>, count_max <dbl>
recipe_qc(filtered, group_by = "RiskGroup2")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 13
#>   group_by   group     n n_zero pct_zero pct_all_zero pct_singletons
#>   <chr>      <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 NA         NA    43368  30986     71.4         0              0   
#> 2 RiskGroup2 hts   11398   8117     71.2         7.19          12.6 
#> 3 RiskGroup2 msm   27800  19912     71.6         2.52           6.12
#> 4 RiskGroup2 pwid   4170   2957     70.9        18.7           15.8 
#> # ℹ 6 more variables: pct_doubletons <dbl>, n_samples <dbl>,
#> #   lib_size_min <dbl>, lib_size_max <dbl>, count_mean <dbl>, count_max <dbl>

Order matters. An abundance threshold expressed relative to all reads uses the total remaining at that point in the sequence. Resampling before a prevalence filter can change which taxa pass it. Specify the intended order explicitly, and remember that engines may also apply their own internal filters. A shared input does not make every engine’s tested-feature set or assumptions identical.

Choose a filtering predicate

The convenience wrappers apply across-sample criteria to each stored taxon:

Step Criterion for retaining a taxon
step_filter_by_prevalence(threshold) Proportion of samples with nonzero abundance is strictly greater than the threshold.
step_filter_by_abundance(threshold) Its total abundance is strictly greater than the threshold times the total abundance of the current table.
step_filter_by_variance(threshold) Its across-sample variance is strictly greater than the threshold, on the stored abundance scale.
step_filter_by_rarity(threshold) Proportion of samples with nonzero abundance is strictly below the threshold.

step_filter_by_rarity() selects rare taxa; it does not remove rare taxa. Use step_filter_by_prevalence() for that purpose. The variance threshold is not a proportion and depends on the abundance units.

For a custom rule, step_filter_taxa() accepts a function with exactly one argument named x and no default. This example includes taxa exactly on the 3% boundary, unlike the strict prevalence wrapper above.

custom_rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy) |>
  step_filter_taxa(.f = function(x) sum(x > 0) >= 0.03 * length(x))

The same predicate may be supplied as a character string:

custom_string_rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy) |>
  step_filter_taxa(.f = "function(x) sum(x > 0) >= 0.03 * length(x)")

Both forms return a recipe, not filtered data or a logical vector. The predicate must return one logical value when applied to each abundance vector during prep(); the wrapper has no prune argument.

To keep recipes safely serializable, the predicate body must be a single expression. Braces, assignments, external variables, namespace-qualified calls, user-defined helpers and lists of functions are not supported, even in local R use. Write thresholds as literal numbers. Accepted expressions include arithmetic, comparisons, logical operators and approved summaries such as sum, mean, median, var and sd; see ?step_filter_taxa for the complete syntax and supported na.rm arguments. The restrictions are checked when the step is added, not only on export.

Rarefaction is optional

The workflow above does not rarefy. step_rarefaction() is available when an explicitly chosen analysis calls for shared equal-depth resampling:

rarefied_rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy) |>
  step_rarefaction()
rarefied <- prep(rarefied_rec, parallel = FALSE)

This is not a general recommendation to normalize DA inputs by rarefaction. Subsampling discards observations and changes the data supplied to downstream methods. Select preprocessing in the context of the scientific question and the methods’ assumptions; equal library sizes do not guarantee valid inference. rarefaction_help() describes the cautions in more detail.

Some DA steps also accept rarefy = TRUE to resample only for that step, rather than altering the shared preprocessing data. For those configured DA steps, the informational note about rarefaction’s controversy appears during prep(), not when the step is added. A shared step_rarefaction() and a method-specific rarefy option are different configurations; do not combine them unless repeat resampling is intentional.

For selecting a central statistical model after defining preprocessing, see Statistical models and contrasts.
